title: The Vanishing Sockets
subtitle: Unhandled code exceptions bypass connection release, freezing an idle database

brief.narrative: During the evening precinct shift change at 17:00, officers check in hundreds of bags of narcotics, firearms, and stolen goods at the Evidence Locker API. Suddenly, the API grinds to a dead halt. Every evidence check-in and lookup begins timing out after 30 seconds with 'HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout'. Operations engineers immediately suspect the PostgreSQL database has crashed. But when they inspect the database server, it is completely idle: CPU utilization is at 3%, memory is at 18%, and disk read/write IOPS are at zero. The database is virtually asleep. However, application server metrics reveal a critical anomaly: the HikariCP database connection pool is 100% full (100 out of 100 connections in use) and 1,840 incoming requests are jammed in the pool wait queue. A new handheld barcode scanner deployed this morning occasionally outputs malformed payload strings beginning with '#BAD#'. When this occurs, an unhandled JSON parsing exception is thrown inside an asynchronous promise after `pool.getConnection()` was called, skipping past the `conn.release()` statement. Every invalid scan permanently leaks an open database socket until the pool completely runs dry.
symptoms: Evidence API response times soared from 25ms to 30,000ms (504 Gateway Timeout)
Database server CPU is at 3% idle with near-zero disk I/O
Application connection pool is 100% starved: active_connections = 100/100, idle = 0, queue_depth = 1,840
Hundreds of evidence intake lockers across 5 precincts cannot lock or log chain-of-custody items
brief.objective: Diagnose why an idle database is starved of connections, and implement robust connection pool lifecycle controls and leak prevention.

rootCause.question: What is the root cause of the Evidence Locker API freezing with gateway timeouts while the database is idle?

options.text: Connection Pool Leak: An unhandled JSON parsing exception bypassed the connection release block, permanently leaking database sockets until all pool connections were exhausted
options.feedback: Correct! This is a classic Database Connection Pool Leak. When the application acquired a connection via `pool.getConnection()`, an unhandled JSON parsing error was thrown before or outside the cleanup block. Because `conn.release()` (or `conn.close()`) was never executed, the socket remained checked out forever in an 'abandoned' state. Once 100 invalid barcodes leaked all 100 pool slots, all subsequent requests queued up and timed out, even though the database server itself was doing zero work.

options.text: PostgreSQL suffered an out-of-disk condition on the transaction log partition, rejecting new write queries
options.feedback: PostgreSQL logs confirm plenty of free disk space and near-zero disk I/O. The database was completely healthy and had no errors; the problem was entirely inside the application server's connection pool.

options.text: The new barcode scanner triggered an electrical power surge over USB that damaged the precinct network router
options.feedback: The network router was working normally. The barcode scanner merely sent an unexpected string prefix (`#BAD#`) that caused software-level JSON parsing errors in the application code.

options.text: PostgreSQL table locks were held by an unindexed foreign key check during evidence insertion
options.feedback: Database query logs show 0 queries were actively running and no locks were contested. The connections were sitting idle because the application had crashed its thread without returning the connection.

fix.question: What architectural and configuration practices should be applied to prevent connection pool leaks from starving the system?

options.text: Enforce automatic resource cleanup using RAII / try-with-resources, configure strict pool connection timeouts, set maxLifetime, and enable leak detection threshold logging
options.feedback: Correct! Robust connection pool hygiene requires multiple defensive layers: (1) Use language constructs that guarantee cleanup (like try-with-resources in Java, RAII in C++, or `try ... finally { conn.release() }` in TypeScript/Go) so exceptions never bypass release. (2) Configure a leak detection threshold in the connection pool (e.g., HikariCP `leakDetectionThreshold = 5000ms`), which automatically logs a stack trace whenever a thread holds a connection longer than 5 seconds. (3) Set pool `maxLifetime` and strict `connectionTimeout` so abandoned connections are retired.

options.text: Increase the connection pool size from 100 to 10,000 connections so the application never runs out of sockets
options.feedback: Increasing pool size does not fix a leak; it just delays the crash by a few hours while severely degrading database performance. 10,000 connections would consume gigabytes of RAM on the database and overwhelm its process table.

options.text: Deploy an hourly cron job that restarts the application container every 60 minutes to clear leaked connections
options.feedback: Automated container restarts are a dangerous hack, not an engineering fix. Shift-change surges could exhaust all 100 connections in 10 minutes, causing outages long before the hourly restart triggers.

options.text: Filter out the '#BAD#' prefix in frontend JavaScript so invalid barcodes are silently dropped before reaching the server
options.feedback: Client-side filtering does not protect the backend from other errors. If another unexpected error occurs (e.g., network timeout or invalid schema), connections would leak again. The backend resource management must be watertight.
